content: Interventions were instrumental in helping women prepare for various childbirth scenarios and in reconciling the benefits of their actual birth method when it did not align with their preferences. There were no or very minor concerns regarding coherence, and the confidence in the findings was moderate. Seven studies contributed to this evidence, four of which had very minor methodological limitations. The data was derived exclusively from Europe and the Americas, with very minor concerns about coherence. The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends non-clinical interventions to reduce unnecessary cesarean sections. These recommendations are supported by evidence tables from the CERQual framework. For example, Cleeton ER conducted a study on the attitudes and beliefs about childbirth among college students, which demonstrated the impact of educational interventions. Similarly, Shorten et al. developed and tested a decision aid for women who had experienced a previous cesarean section, aiming to support informed decision-making about childbirth methods. Wang et al. created a web-based childbirth education program specifically for mothers considering vaginal birth after cesarean (VBAC). Emmett et al. piloted computer-based decision aids to assist women in choosing their mode of delivery after a previous cesarean section. Farnworth et al. explored decision support for women in similar situations, while Frost et al. conducted qualitative interviews to understand women’s views on decision aids for delivery methods following a prior cesarean. Milne et al. developed and pre-tested a decision board to facilitate informed choices about delivery approaches in uncomplicated pregnancies. David et al. analyzed the content of telephone calls made by women to a dedicated antenatal clinic for next birth after cesarean support. Basso and Monticelli examined the expectations of pregnant women and their partners regarding participation in humanized births. Ramvi and Tangerud conducted a biographical, narrative study on women who had vaginal births after initially requesting cesarean sections due to fear of childbirth. Shorten et al. developed an internet-based decision aid for women choosing between VBAC and planned repeat cesarean. McCants explored the impact of pre-birth education on childbirth decision-making, both in published studies and an unpublished thesis. These studies collectively highlight the importance of non-clinical interventions in reducing unnecessary cesarean sections. Health professionals’ beliefs about birth varied across high-income countries (HICs) and middle-income countries (MICs). Some obstetricians and midwives valued the physiological process of birth and worked collaboratively to support it, intervening only when medically necessary. Others viewed labor and vaginal birth as inherently flawed processes, favoring cesarean sections as a safer alternative. These differing ideologies influenced the emphasis placed on reducing cesarean rates. In MICs, some obstetricians who preferred cesarean sections cited perinatal mortality and morbidity benefits, though this was not universally experienced, particularly among female Chinese obstetricians who had undergone cesarean delivery on maternal request (CDMR) or Iranian obstetricians concerned about managing complications from previous cesareans. Beliefs were shaped by professional training, personal experience, and practice settings. Eight studies had minor methodological limitations, while five had moderate to significant concerns. Data coherence was higher in HICs and MICs, with no data from low-income countries (LICs). Rich data was available from countries such as Iran, China, Nicaragua, the USA, Canada, Finland, Sweden, the Netherlands, Germany, Italy, Ireland, Australia, and the UK. Fear of blame and medico-legal concerns influenced health professionals’ low threshold for performing cesarean sections. This fear was particularly pronounced in North America, where medico-legal concerns were a significant factor in non-compliance with guideline recommendations. Across urban and rural settings, obstetricians and midwives weighed the risks to their professional identity and the potential for poor outcomes against the decision not to intervene. Some professionals welcomed guidelines as a defensible basis for their practice, while others remained committed to intervening only when necessary. Economic incentives also played a role in cesarean section preferences, particularly in private healthcare settings. Doctors in countries like Tanzania, Iran, China, and Nicaragua, as well as midwives in Iran and the USA, highlighted the financial rewards associated with cesarean sections. Some viewed cesareans as more labor-intensive and thus justified higher payments, while others criticized insufficient monetary rewards for staff involved in labor and vaginal births. Health professionals valued the convenience of scheduling cesarean sections, which required less time commitment compared to labor and vaginal births. Some also noted that cesareans were convenient for women for similar reasons, though they acknowledged that not all women preferred this method. Seven studies with minor to moderate methodological limitations contributed to this finding, with high coherence across the data. Beliefs about women’s demands for specific birth methods were reported globally. Some health professionals believed women now view cesarean sections as a consumer choice, while others attributed rising cesarean rates to women’s lower thresholds for opting for cesareans during labor. Factors such as rising body mass index (BMI), advanced maternal age, sedentary lifestyles, and Western diseases were perceived as diminishing women’s innate ability to labor and give birth. Health professionals also noted a lack of antenatal education among women, as well as the influence of families and the abundance of information available online and in the media. The need for high-level infrastructure to support safe VBAC was emphasized by health professionals in HICs. While some were flexible in interpreting guidelines and used available technologies to facilitate VBAC, others, particularly in MICs and LICs, expressed concerns about the lack of human and technological resources. Even in HICs with 24-hour obstetrical and anesthesia coverage, some women were still denied a trial of labor. Views on decision-making authority in cesarean sections varied among obstetricians and midwives. While some accepted a woman’s right to choose, others believed the decision should be shared or made solely by qualified health professionals. Time constraints in practice were noted as a barrier to facilitating informed decision-making. However, in teams with a shared approach, informed decision-making was reported to occur effectively.
